Utility-scale error mitigation with probabilistic error amplification

Usage estimate: 15 minutes on a Heron r2 processor (NOTE: This is an estimate only. Your runtime might vary.)

Learning outcomes

  • Understand the theory behind zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), the different methods to amplify noise, and why probabilistic error amplification (PEA) is preferred for utility-scale experiments.
  • Run ZNE with PEA by using the client-side Estimator primitive with explicit noise learning.
  • Build the same experiment from its components with Qiskit noise learning, Qiskit mitigation, and the Executor primitive.

Prerequisites

  • Read the Error mitigation lesson of the Utility-scale quantum computing course for basic knowledge of using error mitigation in Qiskit.
  • Read the Utility-I lesson of the Utility-scale quantum computing course for more background on the utility-scale experiment used as an example in this tutorial.
  • Read the directed execution model guide for background on the Executor primitive and Samplomatic.

Background

This tutorial demonstrates how to run a utility-scale error mitigation experiment on IBM Quantum® hardware by using zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) with probabilistic error amplification (PEA).

Reference: Y. Kim et al. Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance. Nature 618.7965 (2023)

Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE)

Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) is an error mitigation technique that removes the effects of an unknown noise during circuit execution that can be scaled in a known way.

It assumes expectation values scale with noise by a known function

⟨A(λ)⟩=⟨A(0)⟩+∑k=0makλk+R\langle A(\lambda) \rangle = \langle A(0) \rangle + \sum_{k=0}^{m} a_k \lambda^k + R⟨A(λ)⟩=⟨A(0)⟩+k=0∑m​ak​λk+R

where λ\lambdaλ parameterizes the noise strength and can be amplified.

We can implement ZNE with the following steps:

  1. Amplify circuit noise for several noise factors λ1,λ2,…\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldotsλ1​,λ2​,…
  2. Run every noise-amplified circuit to measure ⟨A(λ1)⟩,…\langle A(\lambda_1)\rangle, \ldots⟨A(λ1​)⟩,…
  3. Extrapolate back to the zero-noise limit ⟨A(0)⟩\langle A(0)\rangle⟨A(0)⟩

Amplify noise for ZNE

The main challenge in successfully implementing ZNE is to have an accurate model for noise in the expectation value and to amplify the noise in a known way.

There are three common ways error amplification is implemented for ZNE.

Pulse stretching
Gate folding
Probabilistic error amplification
Scale pulse duration via calibrationRepeat gates in identity cycles U↦U(U−1U)λ−1/2U\mapsto U(U^{-1}U)^{\lambda-1}/2U↦U(U−1U)λ−1/2Add noise via sampling Pauli channels
Kandala et al. Nature (2019)Shultz et al. PRA (2022)Li & Benjamin PRX (2017)

For utility-scale experiments, probabilistic error amplification (PEA) is the most attractive.

  • Pulse stretching assumes gate noise is proportional to duration, which is typically not true. Calibration is also costly.
  • Gate folding requires large stretch factors that greatly limit the depth of circuits that can be run.
  • PEA can be applied to any circuit that can be run with native noise factor (λ=1\lambda=1λ=1) but requires learning the noise model.

Learn the noise model for PEA

PEA assumes the same layer-based noise model as probabilistic error cancellation (PEC); however, it avoids the sampling overhead that scales exponentially with the circuit noise.

Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
Pauli twirl layers of two-qubit gatesRepeat identity pairs of layers and learn the noiseDerive a fidelity (error for each noise channel)

Reference: E. van den Berg, Z. Minev, A. Kandala, and K. Temme, Probabilistic error cancellation with sparse Pauli-Lindblad models on noisy quantum processors arXiv:2201.09866

Two ways to run PEA

This tutorial runs the same PEA experiment in two ways. Both learn the noise of each unique entangling layer in a separate job, then sample the circuit at several amplified noise levels and extrapolate back to zero noise.

Column 1
Path 1: Estimator with explicit noise learning
Path 2: Qiskit noise learning and Qiskit mitigation
Noise learningNoiseLearnerV3Qiskit noise learning
Noise amplification and readout mitigationConfigured through Estimator optionsPEA and TREX tasks from Qiskit mitigation
ExecutionThe client-side Estimator builds and submits an Executor job for youYou build a Samplomatic QuantumProgram and submit it to the Executor yourself
Best forA compact workflow with minimal codeFull control over boxing, learning, and extrapolation, and combining PEA with other techniques

Since qiskit-ibm-runtime v0.50, the Estimator primitive runs its pre- and post-processing on the client side and no longer learns the layer noise implicitly. Path 1 therefore learns the noise in a separate step before running the Estimator. See Migrate from server-side to client-side Sampler and Estimator for details.

Requirements

Before starting this tutorial, be sure you have the following installed:

  • Qiskit SDK v2.0 or later, with visualization support
  • Qiskit Runtime v0.50 or later (pip install qiskit-ibm-runtime)
  • Samplomatic (pip install samplomatic)
  • Qiskit mitigation (pip install qiskit-mitigation)
  • Qiskit noise learning (pip install "git+https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-noise-learning@main")

Setup

In the cell below, import relevant packages and create some helper functions to construct the circuits for the Trotterized time evolution of a two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model that adheres to the topology of the backend.

from __future__ import annotations
from collections.abc import Sequence
from collections import defaultdict
import numpy as np
import rustworkx
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from qiskit.circuit import QuantumCircuit, Parameter
from qiskit.circuit.library import CXGate, CZGate, ECRGate
from qiskit.providers import Backend
from qiskit.visualization import plot_error_map
from qiskit.transpiler import generate_preset_pass_manager
from qiskit.quantum_info import SparsePauliOp
from qiskit.primitives import PubResult

from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService


"""Trotter circuit generation"""


def remove_qubit_couplings(
    couplings: Sequence[tuple[int, int]], qubits: Sequence[int] | None = None
) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    """Remove qubits from a coupling list.

    Args:
        couplings: A sequence of qubit couplings.
        qubits: Optional, the qubits to remove.

    Returns:
        The input couplings with the specified qubits removed.
    """
    if qubits is None:
        return couplings
    qubits = set(qubits)
    return [edge for edge in couplings if not qubits.intersection(edge)]


def coupling_qubits(
    *couplings: Sequence[tuple[int, int]],
    allowed_qubits: Sequence[int] | None = None,
) -> list[int]:
    """Return a sorted list of all qubits involved in one or more couplings lists.

    Args:
        couplings: one or more coupling lists.
        allowed_qubits: Optional, the allowed qubits to include. If None all
            qubits are allowed.

    Returns:
        The intersection of all qubits in the couplings and the allowed qubits.
    """
    qubits = set()
    for edges in couplings:
        for edge in edges:
            qubits.update(edge)
    if allowed_qubits is not None:
        qubits = qubits.intersection(allowed_qubits)
    return list(qubits)


def construct_layer_couplings(
    backend: Backend,
) -> list[list[tuple[int, int]]]:
    """Separate a coupling map into disjoint 2-qubit gate layers.

    Args:
        backend: A backend to construct layer couplings for.

    Returns:
        A list of disjoint layers of directed couplings for the input coupling map.
    """
    coupling_graph = backend.coupling_map.graph.to_undirected(
        multigraph=False
    )
    edge_coloring = rustworkx.graph_bipartite_edge_color(coupling_graph)

    layers = defaultdict(list)
    for edge_idx, color in edge_coloring.items():
        layers[color].append(
            coupling_graph.get_edge_endpoints_by_index(edge_idx)
        )
    layers = [sorted(layers[i]) for i in sorted(layers.keys())]

    return layers


def entangling_layer(
    gate_2q: str,
    couplings: Sequence[tuple[int, int]],
    qubits: Sequence[int] | None = None,
) -> QuantumCircuit:
    """Generating a entangling layer for the specified couplings.

    This corresponds to a Trotter layer for a ZZ Ising term with angle Pi/2.

    Args:
        gate_2q: The 2-qubit basis gate for the layer, should be "cx", "cz", or "ecr".
        couplings: A sequence of qubit couplings to add CX gates to.
        qubits: Optional, the physical qubits for the layer. Any couplings involving
            qubits not in this list will be removed. If None the range up to the largest
            qubit in the couplings will be used.

    Returns:
        The QuantumCircuit for the entangling layer.
    """
    # Get qubits and convert to set to order
    if qubits is None:
        qubits = range(1 + max(coupling_qubits(couplings)))
    qubits = set(qubits)

    # Mapping of physical qubit to virtual qubit
    qubit_mapping = {q: i for i, q in enumerate(qubits)}

    # Convert couplings to indices for virtual qubits
    indices = [
        [qubit_mapping[i] for i in edge]
        for edge in couplings
        if qubits.issuperset(edge)
    ]

    # Layer circuit on virtual qubits
    circuit = QuantumCircuit(len(qubits))

    # Get 2-qubit basis gate and pre and post rotation circuits
    gate2q = None
    pre = QuantumCircuit(2)
    post = QuantumCircuit(2)

    if gate_2q == "cx":
        gate2q = CXGate()
        # Pre-rotation
        pre.sdg(0)
        pre.z(1)
        pre.sx(1)
        pre.s(1)
        # Post-rotation
        post.sdg(1)
        post.sxdg(1)
        post.s(1)
    elif gate_2q == "ecr":
        gate2q = ECRGate()
        # Pre-rotation
        pre.z(0)
        pre.s(1)
        pre.sx(1)
        pre.s(1)
        # Post-rotation
        post.x(0)
        post.sdg(1)
        post.sxdg(1)
        post.s(1)
    elif gate_2q == "cz":
        gate2q = CZGate()
        # Identity pre-rotation
        # Post-rotation
        post.sdg([0, 1])
    else:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Invalid 2-qubit basis gate {gate_2q}, should be 'cx', 'cz', or 'ecr'"
        )

    # Add 1Q pre-rotations
    for inds in indices:
        circuit.compose(pre, qubits=inds, inplace=True)

    # Use barriers around 2-qubit basis gate to specify a layer for PEA noise learning
    circuit.barrier()
    for inds in indices:
        circuit.append(gate2q, (inds[0], inds[1]))
    circuit.barrier()

    # Add 1Q post-rotations after barrier
    for inds in indices:
        circuit.compose(post, qubits=inds, inplace=True)

    # Add physical qubits as metadata
    circuit.metadata["physical_qubits"] = tuple(qubits)

    return circuit


def trotter_circuit(
    theta: Parameter | float,
    layer_couplings: Sequence[Sequence[tuple[int, int]]],
    num_steps: int,
    gate_2q: str | None = "cx",
    backend: Backend | None = None,
    qubits: Sequence[int] | None = None,
) -> QuantumCircuit:
    """Generate a Trotter circuit for the 2D Ising

    Args:
        theta: The angle parameter for X.
        layer_couplings: A list of couplings for each entangling layer.
        num_steps: the number of Trotter steps.
        gate_2q: The 2-qubit basis gate to use in entangling layers.
            Can be "cx", "cz", "ecr", or None if a backend is provided.
        backend: A backend to get the 2-qubit basis gate from, if provided
            will override the basis_gate field.
        qubits: Optional, the allowed physical qubits to truncate the
            couplings to. If None the range up to the largest
            qubit in the couplings will be used.

    Returns:
        The Trotter circuit.
    """
    if backend is not None:
        try:
            basis_gates = backend.configuration().basis_gates
        except AttributeError:
            basis_gates = backend.basis_gates
        for gate in ["cx", "cz", "ecr"]:
            if gate in basis_gates:
                gate_2q = gate
                break

    # If no qubits, get the largest qubit from all layers and
    # specify the range so the same one is used for all layers.
    if qubits is None:
        qubits = range(1 + max(coupling_qubits(layer_couplings)))

    # Generate the entangling layers
    layers = [
        entangling_layer(gate_2q, couplings, qubits=qubits)
        for couplings in layer_couplings
    ]

    # Construct the circuit for a single Trotter step
    num_qubits = len(qubits)
    trotter_step = QuantumCircuit(num_qubits)
    trotter_step.rx(theta, range(num_qubits))
    for layer in layers:
        trotter_step.compose(layer, range(num_qubits), inplace=True)

    # Construct the circuit for the specified number of Trotter steps
    circuit = QuantumCircuit(num_qubits)
    for _ in range(num_steps):
        circuit.rx(theta, range(num_qubits))
        for layer in layers:
            circuit.compose(layer, range(num_qubits), inplace=True)

    circuit.metadata["physical_qubits"] = tuple(qubits)
    return circuit


"""Result visualization functions"""


def plot_trotter_results(
    pub_result: PubResult,
    angles: Sequence[float],
    plot_noise_factors: Sequence[float] | None = None,
    plot_extrapolator: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    exact: np.ndarray = None,
    title: str | None = None,
    close: bool = True,
):
    """Plot average magnetization from ZNE result data.
    Args:
        pub_result: The PubResult for the PEA experiment.
        angles: The Rx angle values for the experiment.
        plot_noise_factors: If provided, plot the unextrapolated data for the noise factors.
        plot_extrapolator: If provided, plot the result of each extrapolator.
        exact: Optional, the exact values to include in the plot. Should be a 1D
            array-like where the values represent exact magnetization.
        title: Optional, the title of the plot.
        close: Close the Matplotlib figure before returning.
    Returns:
        The figure.
    """
    data = pub_result.data

    evs = data.evs
    num_qubits = evs.shape[0]
    num_params = evs.shape[1]
    angles = np.asarray(angles).ravel()
    if angles.shape != (num_params,):
        raise ValueError(
            f"Incorrect number of angles for input data {angles.size} != {num_params}"
        )

    # Take average magnetization of qubits and its standard error
    x_vals = angles / np.pi
    y_vals = np.mean(evs, axis=0)
    y_errs = np.std(evs, axis=0) / np.sqrt(num_qubits)

    fig, _ = plt.subplots(1, 1)

    # Plot auto method
    plt.errorbar(x_vals, y_vals, y_errs, fmt="o-", label="ZNE (automatic)")

    # Plot individual extrapolator results
    if plot_extrapolator:
        y_vals_extrap = np.mean(data.evs_extrapolated, axis=0)
        y_errs_extrap = np.std(data.evs_extrapolated, axis=0) / np.sqrt(
            num_qubits
        )
        for i, extrap in enumerate(plot_extrapolator):
            plt.errorbar(
                x_vals,
                y_vals_extrap[:, i, 0],
                y_errs_extrap[:, i, 0],
                fmt="s-.",
                alpha=0.5,
                label=f"ZNE ({extrap})",
            )

    # Plot raw results
    if plot_noise_factors:
        y_vals_raw = np.mean(data.evs_noise_factors, axis=0)
        y_errs_raw = np.std(data.evs_noise_factors, axis=0) / np.sqrt(
            num_qubits
        )
        for i, nf in enumerate(plot_noise_factors):
            plt.errorbar(
                x_vals,
                y_vals_raw[:, i],
                y_errs_raw[:, i],
                fmt="d:",
                alpha=0.5,
                label=f"Raw (nf={nf:.1f})",
            )

    # Plot exact data
    if exact is not None:
        plt.plot(x_vals, exact, "--", color="black", alpha=0.5, label="Exact")

    plt.ylim(-0.1, 1.2)
    plt.xlabel("θ/π")
    plt.ylabel(r"$\overline{\langle Z \rangle}$")
    plt.legend()
    plt.title(
        title
        or f"Error Mitigated Average Magnetization for Rx(θ) [{num_qubits}-qubit]"
    )
    if close:
        plt.close(fig)
    return fig


def plot_path_comparison(
    pub_results: dict[str, PubResult],
    angles: Sequence[float],
    exact: np.ndarray = None,
    close: bool = True,
):
    """Compare the mitigated and unmitigated average magnetization of several results.
    Args:
        pub_results: The PubResults to compare, keyed by their label.
        angles: The Rx angle values for the experiment.
        exact: Optional, the exact values to include in the plot.
        close: Close the Matplotlib figure before returning.
    Returns:
        The figure.
    """
    x_vals = np.asarray(angles).ravel() / np.pi
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1)
    for i, (label, pub_result) in enumerate(pub_results.items()):
        color = f"C{i}"
        num_qubits = pub_result.data.evs.shape[0]
        # Mitigated (zero-noise extrapolated) values
        evs = pub_result.data.evs
        ax.errorbar(
            x_vals,
            np.mean(evs, axis=0),
            np.std(evs, axis=0) / np.sqrt(num_qubits),
            fmt="o-",
            color=color,
            label=f"{label}: ZNE",
        )
        # Unmitigated values at the native noise factor (nf=1)
        raw = pub_result.data.evs_noise_factors[..., 0]
        ax.errorbar(
            x_vals,
            np.mean(raw, axis=0),
            np.std(raw, axis=0) / np.sqrt(num_qubits),
            fmt="d:",
            color=color,
            alpha=0.5,
            label=f"{label}: raw (nf=1.0)",
        )
    if exact is not None:
        ax.plot(x_vals, exact, "--", color="black", alpha=0.5, label="Exact")
    ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.2)
    ax.set_xlabel("θ/π")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$\overline{\langle Z \rangle}$")
    ax.legend()
    ax.set_title("Comparison of the two PEA workflows")
    if close:
        plt.close(fig)
    return fig


def plot_qubit_zne_data(
    pub_result: PubResult,
    angles: Sequence[float],
    qubit: int,
    noise_factors: Sequence[float],
    extrapolator: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    extrapolated_noise_factors: Sequence[float] | None = None,
    num_cols: int | None = None,
    close: bool = True,
):
    """Plot ZNE extrapolation data for specific virtual qubit
    Args:
        pub_result: The PubResult for the PEA experiment.
        angles: The Rx theta angles used for the experiment.
        qubit: The virtual qubit index to plot.
        noise_factors: the raw noise factors.
        extrapolator: The extrapolator metadata for multiple extrapolators.
        extrapolated_noise_factors: The noise factors used for extrapolation.
        num_cols: The number of columns for the generated subplots.
        close: Close the Matplotlib figure before returning.
    Returns:
        The Matplotlib figure.
    """
    data = pub_result.data

    evs_auto = data.evs[qubit]
    stds_auto = data.stds[qubit]
    evs_extrap = data.evs_extrapolated[qubit]
    stds_extrap = data.stds_extrapolated[qubit]
    evs_raw = data.evs_noise_factors[qubit]
    stds_raw = data.stds_noise_factors[qubit]

    num_params = evs_auto.shape[0]
    angles = np.asarray(angles).ravel()
    if angles.shape != (num_params,):
        raise ValueError(
            f"Incorrect number of angles for input data {angles.size} != {num_params}"
        )

    # Make a square subplot
    num_cols = num_cols or int(np.ceil(np.sqrt(num_params)))
    num_rows = int(np.ceil(num_params / num_cols))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(
        num_rows, num_cols, sharex=True, sharey=True, figsize=(12, 5)
    )
    fig.suptitle(f"ZNE data for virtual qubit {qubit}")

    for pidx, ax in zip(range(num_params), axes.flat):
        # Plot auto extrapolated
        ax.errorbar(
            0,
            evs_auto[pidx],
            stds_auto[pidx],
            fmt="o",
            label="PEA (automatic)",
        )

        # Plot extrapolators
        if (
            extrapolator is not None
            and extrapolated_noise_factors is not None
        ):
            for i, method in enumerate(extrapolator):
                ax.errorbar(
                    extrapolated_noise_factors,
                    evs_extrap[pidx, i],
                    stds_extrap[pidx, i],
                    fmt="-",
                    alpha=0.5,
                    label=f"PEA ({method})",
                )

        # Plot raw
        ax.errorbar(
            noise_factors, evs_raw[pidx], stds_raw[pidx], fmt="d", label="Raw"
        )

        ax.set_yticks([0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2])
        ax.set_ylim(0, max(1, 1.1 * max(evs_auto)))

        ax.set_xticks([0, *noise_factors])
        ax.set_title(f"θ/π = {angles[pidx]/np.pi:.2f}")
        if pidx == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel(r"$\langle Z_{" + str(qubit) + r"} \rangle$")
        if pidx == num_params - 1:
            ax.set_xlabel("Noise Factor")
            ax.legend()
    plt.tight_layout()
    if close:
        plt.close(fig)
    return fig

Small-scale simulator example

This tutorial skips the small-scale simulator example and focuses on a utility-scale experiment. To try PEA with Qiskit mitigation on a local noisy simulator first, see the Zero-noise extrapolation with probabilistic error amplification guide.

Large-scale hardware example

Step 1: Map classical inputs to a quantum problem

Create a parameterized Ising model circuit

Establish a backend

First, choose a backend to run on. This demonstration runs on a backend with at least 127 qubits, but you can modify this to any backend available to you.

service = QiskitRuntimeService()
backend = service.least_busy(
    operational=True, simulator=False, min_num_qubits=127
)
backend

Output:

<IBMBackend('ibm_kingston')>
Define entangling layer couplings

To implement the Trotterized Ising simulation, define three layers of two-qubit gate couplings for the device, to be repeated at each of the Trotter steps. These layers of two-qubit gates are the twirled layers whose noise you need to learn to implement mitigation.

layer_couplings = construct_layer_couplings(backend)
for i, layer in enumerate(layer_couplings):
    print(f"Layer {i}:\n{layer}\n")

Remove bad qubits

Look at the error map for the backend and remove "bad" qubits from your experiment. The following code removes every qubit that is part of a two-qubit gate with an error of 5% or higher, or that has a readout error of 20% or higher.

# Plot gate error map
# NOTE: These can change over time, so your results may look different
plot_error_map(backend)

Output:

# NOTE: Calibration data can change over time, so your selection might differ
max_2q_error = 0.05
max_readout_error = 0.2

gate_2q = next(
    gate
    for gate in ["cz", "ecr", "cx"]
    if gate in backend.target.operation_names
)
bad_qubits = set()
for qubits, props in backend.target[gate_2q].items():
    if props is None or props.error is None or props.error >= max_2q_error:
        bad_qubits.update(qubits)
for (qubit,), props in backend.target["measure"].items():
    if (
        props is None
        or props.error is None
        or props.error >= max_readout_error
    ):
        bad_qubits.add(qubit)

good_qubits = sorted(set(range(backend.num_qubits)).difference(bad_qubits))
print(f"Removed qubits: {sorted(bad_qubits)}")
print(f"Number of physical qubits used: {len(good_qubits)}")

Output:

Removed qubits: [72, 85, 86, 87, 111, 112, 113, 116, 120, 121, 130, 131, 145, 146, 147]
Number of physical qubits used: 141
Main Trotter circuit generation
num_steps = 6
theta = Parameter("theta")
circuit = trotter_circuit(
    theta, layer_couplings, num_steps, qubits=good_qubits, backend=backend
)

Create a list of parameter values to be assigned later

num_params = 12

# 12 parameter values for Rx between [0, pi/2].
# Reshape to outer product broadcast with observables
parameter_values = np.linspace(0, np.pi / 2, num_params).reshape(
    (num_params, 1)
)

Step 2: Optimize problem for quantum hardware execution

ISA circuit

Before running the circuit on hardware, optimize it for hardware execution. This process involves a few steps:

  • Pick a qubit layout that maps the virtual qubits of your circuit to physical qubits on the hardware.
  • Insert swap gates as needed to route interactions between qubits that are not connected.
  • Translate the gates in our circuit to Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) instructions that can directly be executed on the hardware.
  • Perform circuit optimizations to minimize the circuit depth and gate count.

Although the transpiler built into Qiskit can perform all of these steps, this tutorial demonstrates building the utility-scale Trotter circuit in a ground-up fashion. Select the good physical qubits and define entangling layers on connected qubit pairs from those selected qubits. Nonetheless, you still need to translate non-ISA gates in the circuit and avail any circuit optimization offered by the transpiler.

Transpile your circuit for the chosen backend by creating a pass manager and then running the pass manager on the circuit. Also, fix the initial layout of the circuit to the already selected good_qubits. An easy way to create a pass manager is to use the generate_preset_pass_manager function. See Transpile with pass managers for a more detailed explanation of transpiling with pass managers.

pm = generate_preset_pass_manager(
    backend=backend,
    initial_layout=good_qubits,
    layout_method="trivial",
    optimization_level=1,
)

isa_circuit = pm.run(circuit)

ISA observables

Next, create all weight-1 ⟨Z⟩\langle Z \rangle⟨Z⟩ observables for each virtual qubit by padding the necessary number of ⟨I⟩\langle I \rangle⟨I⟩ terms.

observables = []
num_qubits = len(good_qubits)
for q in range(num_qubits):
    observables.append(
        SparsePauliOp("I" * (num_qubits - q - 1) + "Z" + "I" * q)
    )

The transpilation process has mapped the virtual qubits of your circuit to physical qubits on the hardware. The information about the qubit layout is stored in the layout attribute of the transpiled circuit. Your observable is also defined in terms of the virtual qubits, so you need to apply this layout to the observable. This is done using the apply_layout method of SparsePauliOp.

In the isa_observables list used in Path 1, each observable is wrapped in a list. This broadcasts the observables with the parameter values so that each qubit observable is measured for each theta value. Find the broadcasting rules for primitives in the primitives documentation. The PEA task used in Path 2 takes a flat list of observables and broadcasts them with the parameter values in the same way.

flat_isa_observables = [
    obs.apply_layout(layout=isa_circuit.layout) for obs in observables
]
isa_observables = [[obs] for obs in flat_isa_observables]

Step 3: Execute using Qiskit primitives

Both paths use the same circuit, observables, parameter values, noise factors, and number of randomizations, so you can compare their results in Step 4.

Experiment settings

The following settings are shared by both paths.

  • num_randomizations and shots_per_randomization: The number of Pauli-twirled instances of each circuit and the number of shots for each instance. The injected PEA noise is sampled once per randomization, so the statistical error of PEA is controlled mostly by the number of randomizations.
  • learning_pair_depths: The numbers of repeated identity pairs of each layer in the noise-learning circuits.
  • noise_factors: The factors by which to amplify the learned noise. A noise factor of 1 corresponds to the native noise of the circuit.
  • extrapolators: The models used to extrapolate to the zero-noise limit, in order of priority.
  • extrapolated_noise_factors: The noise factors at which to evaluate the extrapolated models. A value of 0 corresponds to zero-noise extrapolation.
# Mitigation experiment settings
num_randomizations = 300
shots_per_randomization = 64
noise_factors = [1, 1.3, 1.6]
extrapolators = ["exponential", "linear"]
extrapolated_noise_factors = np.linspace(0, max(noise_factors), 20)

# Noise learning settings
num_randomizations_learning = 40
shots_per_randomization_learning = 64
learning_pair_depths = [0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24]

# Job tags for all jobs submitted by this tutorial
job_tags = ["TUT_PEA"]

Path 1: Run PEA with the Estimator and explicit noise learning

Configure Estimator options

Configure the client-side Estimator options needed to run the mitigation experiment. This includes enabling TREX measurement mitigation and ZNE with the PEA amplifier.

from qiskit_ibm_runtime.executor_estimator import Estimator

options = {
    "resilience": {
        # Builtin resilience settings for TREX and ZNE
        "measure_mitigation": True,
        "zne_mitigation": True,
        "zne": {
            "amplifier": "pea",
            "noise_factors": noise_factors,
            "extrapolator": extrapolators,
            "extrapolated_noise_factors": extrapolated_noise_factors.tolist(),
        },
    },
    # Randomization configuration
    "twirling": {
        "num_randomizations": num_randomizations,
        "shots_per_randomization": shots_per_randomization,
        "strategy": "active-accum",
    },
    # Job tag
    "environment": {"job_tags": job_tags},
}

estimator = Estimator(mode=backend, options=options)

The following options control ZNE:

  • amplifier: The method to use when amplifying noise to the intended noise factors. Allowed values are "gate_folding", which amplifies by repeating two-qubit basis gates, and "pea", which amplifies by probabilistic sampling after learning the Pauli-twirled noise model for layers of twirled two-qubit basis gates. Additional options are "gate_folding_front" and "gate_folding_back", which are explained in the API documentation.
  • extrapolated_noise_factors: Specify one or more noise factor values at which to evaluate the extrapolated models. If a sequence of values, the returned results will be array-valued with specified noise factor evaluated for the extrapolation model. A value of 0 corresponds to zero-noise extrapolation.

The active-accum twirling strategy twirls only the qubits that have been active up to each layer. The removed qubits have no gates, so this strategy keeps them out of the twirled layers and out of the noise model. Their unreliable data would otherwise distort the noise learned for their neighbors.

The Estimator can also apply dynamical decoupling. It is left disabled here so that both paths run the same circuits.

Learn the layer noise with NoiseLearnerV3

PEA needs a noise model for each unique layer of entangling gates in the circuit. The find_unique_layers method of the Estimator groups the entangling gates of the PUB into boxes and returns the unique boxed layers. Because of the active-accum twirling strategy, the first two layers of the first Trotter step act on fewer qubits than the later layers, so there are five unique layers in total.

Pass these layers to NoiseLearnerV3, which learns a sparse Pauli-Lindblad noise model for each layer in a separate job.

from qiskit_ibm_runtime import NoiseLearnerV3

pub = (isa_circuit, isa_observables, parameter_values)
layers = estimator.find_unique_layers([pub])
print(f"Number of unique layers to learn: {len(layers)}")

learner_options = {
    "num_randomizations": num_randomizations_learning,
    "shots_per_randomization": shots_per_randomization_learning,
    "layer_pair_depths": learning_pair_depths,
    "environment": {"job_tags": job_tags},
}
learner = NoiseLearnerV3(mode=backend, options=learner_options)
learner_job = learner.run(layers)
print(f"Noise learner job ID {learner_job.job_id()}")

Output:

Number of unique layers to learn: 5
Noise learner job ID db7t8mmr6oqs73889co0

After the noise-learning job finishes, convert its result to PauliLindbladMap objects and pair each map with its layer in the layer_noise_model option. The maps are in the same order as the input layers.

layer_noise_maps = learner_job.result().to_pauli_lindblad_maps()
estimator.options.resilience.layer_noise_model = list(
    zip(layers, layer_noise_maps)
)
Run the experiment
job = estimator.run([pub])
print(f"Job ID {job.job_id()}")

Output:

Job ID db7tdqmil99s73forev0

Path 2: Run PEA with Qiskit noise learning and Qiskit mitigation

In this path, you perform each step of the experiment yourself:

  1. Find the unique layers of the circuit with the PEA task from Qiskit mitigation.
  2. Learn the noise of these layers with Qiskit noise learning.
  3. Prepare a QuantumProgram that samples the circuit at each noise factor, together with a TREX calibration circuit.
  4. Run the program with the Executor primitive.
  5. Extrapolate to the zero-noise limit with the PEA task.
Find the unique layers

The PEA task groups the circuit instructions into annotated boxes with Samplomatic. Each box of entangling gates carries an InjectNoise annotation, whose reference identifies the layer. Pass the same boxing options to every method of the task so that the boxes, and their references, are consistent. Here, the twirling_strategy boxing option matches the twirling strategy used in Path 1.

from qiskit_mitigation import PEA
from samplomatic import InjectNoise
from samplomatic.utils import get_annotation

boxing_options = {"twirling_strategy": "active_accum"}

pea_task = PEA()
# Learn only the layers that PEA injects noise into, not the measurement layer
pea_layers = [
    layer
    for layer in pea_task.find_unique_layers(isa_circuit, boxing_options)
    if get_annotation(layer.operation, InjectNoise)
]
print(f"Number of unique layers to learn: {len(pea_layers)}")

Output:

Number of unique layers to learn: 5
Learn the layer noise with Qiskit noise learning

The prepare_learning_program function builds a QuantumProgram that learns a two-local Pauli-Lindblad noise model for each layer, as well as a model of the readout noise. Its fragment_depths argument plays the same role as the layer_pair_depths option of NoiseLearnerV3. Submit the program to the Executor primitive.

The Qiskit noise learning and Qiskit mitigation packages build Samplomatic QuantumProgram objects. In qiskit-ibm-runtime v0.50, the Executor primitive accepts only the QuantumProgram subclass from qiskit_ibm_runtime.quantum_program, so the following code defines a to_runtime_program helper to convert the programs before you submit them.

Note

Starting with the next release of qiskit-ibm-runtime, Executor.run converts Samplomatic programs automatically, and you can submit them directly.

from qiskit_ibm_runtime import Executor
from qiskit_ibm_runtime.quantum_program import QuantumProgram
from qiskit_noise_learning.protocols import prepare_learning_program


def to_runtime_program(program) -> QuantumProgram:
    """Convert a Samplomatic QuantumProgram to a Qiskit Runtime QuantumProgram."""
    return QuantumProgram(
        shots=program.shots,
        items=program.items,
        noise_maps=program.noise_maps,
        meas_level=program.meas_level,
        passthrough_data=program.passthrough_data,
    )


executor = Executor(
    mode=backend, options={"environment": {"job_tags": job_tags}}
)

learning_program = prepare_learning_program(
    backend,
    pea_layers,
    num_randomizations=num_randomizations_learning,
    shots_per_randomization=shots_per_randomization_learning,
    fragment_depths=learning_pair_depths,
)
learning_job = executor.run(to_runtime_program(learning_program))
print(f"Noise learning job ID {learning_job.job_id()}")

Output:

Noise learning job ID db8er9iraffc73fc8rfg

After the job finishes, fit the noise model with process_learning_result and convert it to one PauliLindbladMap for each layer, keyed by the layer's InjectNoise reference. The restrict_to_qubit_idxs=True argument returns each map on the qubits of its layer only, which is the form that the PEA task expects.

from qiskit_noise_learning.models.utils import split_pauli_lindblad_model
from qiskit_noise_learning.protocols import process_learning_result

fit = process_learning_result(learning_job.result())
noise_model = split_pauli_lindblad_model(fit.model).model
learned_noise = noise_model.to_pauli_lindblad_maps(
    fit.model_data, restrict_to_qubit_idxs=True
)

for ref, noise_map in learned_noise.items():
    print(
        f"Layer {ref}: {noise_map.num_qubits} qubits, "
        f"{len(noise_map.rates)} generators, "
        f"sum of rates {np.sum(noise_map.rates):.3f}"
    )

Output:

Layer r079A: 102 qubits, 1116 generators, sum of rates 0.264
Layer rb3cA: 134 qubits, 1680 generators, sum of rates 0.308
Layer r0fdA: 141 qubits, 1764 generators, sum of rates 0.359
Layer r502A: 141 qubits, 1764 generators, sum of rates 0.307
Layer r615A: 141 qubits, 1764 generators, sum of rates 0.316
Prepare the PEA and TREX program

Create a TREX task and pass it to PEA.prepare. This adds measurement twirling to the PEA circuit, which TREX requires. Then add a TREX calibration circuit to the same program with TREX.prepare, so that the readout noise is learned while the mitigated circuits run. The PEA task samples the circuit at each noise factor by injecting the learned noise, scaled by the noise factor minus one, after each layer.

from qiskit_mitigation import TREX

trex = TREX()
pea_program = pea_task.prepare(
    circuit=isa_circuit,
    observables=flat_isa_observables,
    parameters=parameter_values,
    custom_boxing_options=boxing_options,
    num_randomizations=num_randomizations,
    shots_per_randomization=shots_per_randomization,
    trex=trex,
    noise_maps=learned_noise,
    noise_factors=noise_factors,
    extrapolator=extrapolators,
    extrapolated_noise_factors=extrapolated_noise_factors.tolist(),
)
pea_program = trex.prepare(
    num_randomizations=num_randomizations,
    quantum_program=pea_program,
    custom_boxing_options=boxing_options,
)
print(f"Number of program items: {len(pea_program.items)}")

Output:

Number of program items: 2
Run the experiment
pea_job = executor.run(to_runtime_program(pea_program))
print(f"Job ID {pea_job.job_id()}")

Output:

Job ID db8f1eur6oqs7389a5g0

Step 4: Post-process and return result in desired classical format

Once the experiments are finished, you can view your results. Fetch the raw and mitigated expectation values from each path and compare them with exact results. Then, plot the expectation values, both mitigated (extrapolated) and raw, averaged over all qubits for each parameter. Finally, plot expectation values for your choice of individual qubits.

Path 1 results

primitive_result = job.result()
General result shapes and metadata

The PrimitiveResult object contains a list-like structure of PubResult objects. As we submit only one PUB to the estimator, the PrimitiveResult contains a single PubResult object.

The PUB (primitive unified bloc) result expectation values and standard errors are array-valued. For estimator jobs with ZNE, there are several data fields of expectation values and standard errors available in the PubResult's DataBin container. We will briefly discuss the data fields for expectation values here (similar data fields are available for standard errors (stds) as well).

  1. pub_result.data.evs: Expectation values corresponding to the zero noise (based on heuristically best extrapolation).
    • The first axis is the virtual qubit index for observable ⟨Zi⟩\langle Z_i\rangle⟨Zi​⟩ (one for each qubit)
    • The second axis indexes the parameter value for θ\thetaθ (121212 parameter values)
  2. pub_result.data.evs_extrapolated: Expectation values for extrapolated noise factors for every extrapolator. This array has two additional axes.
    • The third axis indexes the extrapolation methods (222 extrapolators, exponential and linear)
    • The last axis indexes the extrapolated_noise_factors (202020 extrapolation points specified in the option)
  3. pub_result.data.evs_noise_factors: Raw expectation values for each noise factor.
    • The third axis indexes the raw noise_factors (333 factors)
pub_result = primitive_result[0]

print(
    f"{pub_result.data.evs.shape=}\n"
    f"{pub_result.data.evs_extrapolated.shape=}\n"
    f"{pub_result.data.evs_noise_factors.shape=}\n"
)

Output:

pub_result.data.evs.shape=(141, 12)
pub_result.data.evs_extrapolated.shape=(141, 12, 2, 20)
pub_result.data.evs_noise_factors.shape=(141, 12, 3)

Path 2 results

Pass the result of the Path 2 job to the postprocess method of the PEA task. Because the program contains the TREX calibration circuit, postprocess uses its data to correct the readout errors before it extrapolates. The returned PubResult has the same data fields and shapes as the Estimator result.

pea_result = pea_task.postprocess(pea_job.result())

print(
    f"{pea_result.data.evs.shape=}\n"
    f"{pea_result.data.evs_extrapolated.shape=}\n"
    f"{pea_result.data.evs_noise_factors.shape=}\n"
)

pea_result.data.evs_extrapolated.shape=(141, 12, 2, 20)

Plot Trotter simulation results

The following code creates a plot for each path to compare the raw and mitigated experiment results against the exact solution.

fig = plot_trotter_results(
    pub_result,
    parameter_values,
    plot_extrapolator=extrapolators,
    plot_noise_factors=noise_factors,
    exact=exact_data,
    title="Path 1: Estimator with NoiseLearnerV3",
)
display(fig)

Output:

fig = plot_trotter_results(
    pea_result,
    parameter_values,
    plot_extrapolator=extrapolators,
    plot_noise_factors=noise_factors,
    exact=exact_data,
    title="Path 2: Qiskit noise learning and Qiskit mitigation",
)
display(fig)

Output:

In both paths, the noisy (noise factor nf=1.0) values are biased below the exact values, while the mitigated values are close to the exact values, demonstrating the utility of the PEA-based mitigation technique.

Compare the two paths

The following plot shows the mitigated and unmitigated results of both paths together.

fig = plot_path_comparison(
    {"Path 1": pub_result, "Path 2": pea_result},
    parameter_values,
    exact=exact_data,
)
display(fig)

Recommendations

If you found this work interesting, you might be interested in the following material:

  • A tutorial focused on combining error mitigation techniques.
  • Detailed documentation on the error mitigation techniques available in Qiskit.
